anchor_reviews.tex_anchor: The direct object is accusative. In the following example, \textbf{geseah} is supplied: “saw,” third-person singular preterite. Its conjugation is not required here.[12]
anchor_reviews.semantic_observation: The actual introductory paragraph states that a direct object is accusative and identifies geseah as supplied. The worked example immediately follows; the route is to explanation, not to an exercise.
The article heading introduces the complete case/gender table, agreement rule, and explicitly bounded instrumental reference forms. All three existing subentry meanings remain supported.

Basic constructions contains the actual rules and worked models for nominative predicates, article omission, coordination, locative on + dative and dependent genitives. The existing broad section route remains appropriate.

Duration, syllables and stress contains consonant-length conditions, audible unstressed vowels, syllable counting and prefix stress. Worked words remain explanatory examples.

The expanded c/g subsection begins the ordered decision procedure: combinations, initial and noninitial c, y-valued g, then stopped/continuous non-y g. The broad palatal/hard-values route remains here; only the narrower continuous-g subentry is redirected.

The voice section gives the ordinary f/s/th environments and supplied exceptions, supporting the voicing subentry directly.

anchor_reviews.tex_anchor: The recipient of a gift is dative; the thing given is accusative. The supplied \textbf{sealde} means “gave,” third-person singular preterite.[12]

anchor_reviews.tex_anchor: The same dependent may stand inside a prepositional phrase. Its genitive does not change the case required for the head.

Strong-neuter explanations and tables support N/A identity, -u/zero and stem weight, exceptional trēo, and the selected disyllabic patterns. Vowel length remains distinguished from syllable weight.

anchor_reviews.tex_anchor: Use \textbf{fram + dative} for what something is separated from. The supplied \textbf{gedǣlde} means “separated/\allowbreak{}divided,” third-person singular preterite.[12]
anchor_reviews.semantic_observation: The source paragraph still explains separation with fram + dative. The new exact TeX string adds only allowbreak inside separated/divided; its semantic destination is unchanged.
Simple vowels contains the value table, rounded-front articulation, and explicitly stressed a before nasal consonants. The same teaching scope remains available.

The actual revised Unit 2 heading still introduces full personal declensions. Nominatives are explicitly review; oblique cells complete the system, with first/second genitives bounded as reference. Its existing complete-declension route is preserved.

Actual table T17 contains all ten selected nominative subject forms: ic/wit/wē, ðū/git/gē, hē/hit/hēo/hīe. The marker targets the paradigm itself. Labels restrict this new route to subject forms; they do not imply full oblique declensions.

anchor_reviews.tex_anchor: In the third-person singular, \textbf{hē, hit, hēo} normally refer to masculine, neuter, and feminine nouns respectively. Use grammatical gender when referring to a thing: a feminine noun need not name a female. All plural nouns take \textbf{hīe}. The context identifies which noun the pronoun refers to; gender and number help to check that reference.
anchor_reviews.semantic_observation: The actual paragraph explains hē/hit/hēo by grammatical gender, hīe for plural reference, and the role of context. The new Gender route and expanded Personal pronouns route accurately describe this bounded nominative explanation.

anchor_reviews.tex_anchor: \textbf{1–3 pl.} gives the shared form for \textbf{wē, gē, hīe}. The dual subjects \textbf{wit} and \textbf{git} also take these ordinary plural verb forms: there is no separate dual form of the copula. Use a dual when specifically saying “we two” or “you two”; the ordinary plurals do not exclude a group of two. Cook also gives \textbf{sind, sint} beside the selected \textbf{sindon}.[16]
anchor_reviews.semantic_observation: The actual paragraph immediately after T18 states that wit/git take ordinary plural copula forms and that ordinary plurals can include two. It directly supports both new Unit 1 dual-agreement references while retaining Unit 2 continuation.

anchor_reviews.tex_anchor: For the continuous \textbf{g}, put the back of the tongue near the position for hard \textbf{g}, but leave a narrow gap. Let air pass continuously while the throat vibrates: the sound can be held, unlike the stopped \textbf{g} of \emph{go}. Its phonetic sign is \textbf{[ɣ]}. Do not omit it or substitute \textbf{y}. First selecting the \textbf{y} or non-\textbf{y} branch prevents this rule from changing the final sound of \textbf{dæg} into continuous \textbf{g}.
anchor_reviews.semantic_observation: The actual articulation paragraph describes the voiced continuous back sound and explicitly requires the prior y/non-y choice. The preceding non-y table supplies its environment. This precise target supports continuous g without implying that all noninitial g is continuous.
